title: stateIn / shareIn & Lifecycle-Safe Collection
scopeHtml: Scope: turning cold flows into hot ones (stateIn/shareIn, SharingStarted) and collecting them safely from UI (repeatOnLifecycle, flowWithLifecycle, collectAsStateWithLifecycle).

questions.promptHtml: What do stateIn and shareIn do, and why would you use them instead of just exposing the cold flow from your repository?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand cold vs hot at the mechanism level (who runs the producer, how many times), which drives every later lifecycle question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A cold flow re-runs its producer for every collector. stateIn and shareIn start exactly one collection of the upstream inside a scope I give them, and multicast the results to any number of downstream collectors. stateIn gives me a StateFlow (always has a value, conflated, equality-deduplicated), shareIn gives me a SharedFlow (configurable replay and buffer). I use them so the screen has one upstream, a current value to read synchronously, and survives rotation without re-querying."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cold flow: flow { ... } is a recipe. Each collect executes the lambda again. If a ViewModel exposes repo.observeOrders() (Room or network), every collector (a rotation, a second fragment, a second combine) triggers another query/subscription.

stateIn/shareIn do this:

  1. Launch ONE coroutine in the scope you pass (using the scope's context, so its dispatcher and Job).
  2. That coroutine collects the upstream and pushes each value into an internal MutableStateFlow / MutableSharedFlow.
  3. Return the read-only view (StateFlow / SharedFlow).
  4. The started: SharingStarted policy decides when that coroutine is running.
cold:   collectorA --> [producer run #1]
        collectorB --> [producer run #2]

shared: collectorA --\
                      +--> [MutableStateFlow] <-- [ONE upstream collect in viewModelScope]
        collectorB --/

Lifetime: the sharing coroutine is a child of scope, so it ends when the scope is cancelled (for viewModelScope, at onCleared). It is NOT tied to the number of collectors unless you pick WhileSubscribed.

Signatures (kotlinx.coroutines 1.4+):

  • fun <T> Flow<T>.stateIn(scope: CoroutineScope, started: SharingStarted, initialValue: T): StateFlow<T>
  • suspend fun <T> Flow<T>.stateIn(scope: CoroutineScope): StateFlow<T> (waits for first value)
  • fun <T> Flow<T>.shareIn(scope: CoroutineScope, started: SharingStarted, replay: Int = 0): SharedFlow<T>

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class OrdersViewModel(repo: OrdersRepository) : ViewModel() {
    // BAD: each collector re-runs the DB query / network call
    val coldOrders: Flow<List<Order>> = repo.observeOrders()

    // GOOD: one upstream, current value, survives rotation
    val orders: StateFlow<List<Order>> = repo.observeOrders()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing stateIn makes the upstream "run once forever". With WhileSubscribed it stops and restarts.
  • Passing a short-lived or wrong scope (e.g. a scope created per call) so the sharing coroutine leaks or dies early.
  • Assuming .value triggers the upstream (it does not; see the .value question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does stateIn change which thread the upstream runs on? → The upstream runs in the scope's context (so viewModelScope = Dispatchers.Main.immediate), not on the collector's thread. Use flowOn upstream of stateIn for IO work.
  2. Can I stateIn a flow that completes? → Yes, the StateFlow just stops updating and keeps the last value; it never completes for collectors.
  3. What happens to exceptions in the upstream? → They fail the sharing coroutine in your scope, not the collector. See the error-handling chunk and Q611 here.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "converts cold flow to hot flow." Senior: states who launches the collection, in which context/scope, what ends it, that the policy (SharingStarted) controls start/stop, and names the production consequence (duplicate queries, leaks, restart cost).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team exposed a Retrofit-backed flow {} directly; three collectors on one screen meant three identical API calls per screen open, tripling backend load until stateIn was added.

questions.promptHtml: Explain SharingStarted.Eagerly, Lazily, and WhileSubscribed. When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The three options map directly to battery, memory and freshness trade-offs. Wrong choice is the root of most hot-flow leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Eagerly starts the upstream immediately and never stops until the scope dies. Lazily starts when the first subscriber appears and also never stops. WhileSubscribed starts on the first subscriber and stops when the subscriber count drops to zero, after an optional timeout. For UI state in a ViewModel I default to WhileSubscribed(5_000). Eagerly/Lazily are for state that must keep updating regardless of UI, like an app-level session or cache, and I accept the cost."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SharingStarted is a strategy that turns the subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int> of the shared flow into a stream of commands: START, STOP, STOP_AND_RESET_REPLAY_CACHE.

Strategy Starts Stops Cache reset Use for
Eagerly immediately when stateIn is called only when scope cancelled never state that must be ready before anyone looks (preloading), app-level singletons
Lazily when first subscriber arrives only when scope cancelled never expensive upstream you want on-demand but then kept
WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis=0, replayExpirationMillis=Long.MAX_VALUE) on first subscriber when count == 0 for stopTimeout after replayExpiration more almost all UI state

Note Lazily and Eagerly do not use subscriber count to stop, so a callbackFlow listening to GPS or a socket keeps its resource registered for the whole ViewModel lifetime.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val user = repo.observeUser().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null)       // always on
val feed = repo.observeFeed().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Lazily, emptyList()) // on after first look, then always
val cart = repo.observeCart().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Cart.EMPTY)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Defaulting to Eagerly "to avoid the loading flash" and leaving a Room/GPS/socket upstream alive in the background.
  • Using WhileSubscribed() with no timeout, so rotation tears down and restarts upstream.
  • Forgetting that no collectors means upstream is off, so .value is stale/initial.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which one is the default recommendation from Android docs? → WhileSubscribed(5000) for UI-layer state.
  2. Can I write my own? → Yes, SharingStarted is a fun interface with command(subscriptionCount); see Q609.
  3. Eagerly vs launching a collect in init? → Similar effect; stateIn(Eagerly) also gives you a StateFlow and one-line multicasting.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE recites the three names. Senior ties each to resource lifetime (DB observers, GPS, sockets), explains subscriber count as the signal, and states the cost of each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching one Eagerly location state to WhileSubscribed(5_000) cut background GPS usage on a delivery app (see Q608).

questions.promptHtml: What exactly do stopTimeoutMillis and replayExpirationMillis do in WhileSubscribed? What are the defaults and how do they interact?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates know WhileSubscribed(5000) as a magic string. Seniors know the state machine and when the cache resets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "stopTimeoutMillis is how long after the last subscriber leaves before the upstream is cancelled; default 0. replayExpirationMillis is how long after that stop before the replay cache is reset; default Long.MAX_VALUE, meaning never. For a StateFlow, reset means going back to the initial value. They are sequential: stop at T+stopTimeout, reset at T+stopTimeout+replayExpiration."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Conceptually (this mirrors the library implementation):

subscriptionCount > 0  -> START
subscriptionCount == 0 -> delay(stopTimeout)
                          if replayExpiration > 0: STOP, then delay(replayExpiration)
                          STOP_AND_RESET_REPLAY_CACHE
  • If the count goes back above 0 during the stopTimeout delay, the pending stop is cancelled (transformLatest), so upstream never notices.
  • If it returns after STOP but before reset, upstream restarts, but late subscribers first see the cached (possibly old) value.
  • If replayExpirationMillis = 0, the cache resets immediately at stop.
  • For stateIn, "reset replay cache" sets the StateFlow back to initialValue. (For shareIn, the replay buffer is cleared.)
  • Both params must be non-negative or IllegalArgumentException.

Timeline (stop=5s, replayExp=60s):

t=0   last collector leaves
t=5   STOP     (upstream cancelled; value still cached)
t=65  RESET    (value -> initialValue)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val balance = repo.observeBalance().stateIn(
    scope = viewModelScope,
    started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(
        stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000,
        replayExpirationMillis = 60_000
    ),
    initialValue = Balance.Loading
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking replayExpirationMillis counts from the last emission. It counts from the stop.
  • Assuming default resets to initial on stop. Default keeps stale value forever (until scope dies).
  • Setting replayExpiration to 0 and then seeing a Loading flash on every return from background.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would you want replayExpiration finite? → Avoid showing very stale data (price, balance) as if fresh; after N seconds show Loading/skeleton instead. See Q613.
  2. Is there a performance cost to the timeout? → Upstream (DB observer) stays registered for up to 5 s after leaving.
  3. What if two different screens share one flow? → Count is shared; upstream stops only when both are gone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE knows 5000 for rotation. Senior draws the two-stage timeline, knows reset means initialValue for StateFlow, and chooses expiration by staleness requirements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A finance screen showed a 3-hour old balance for ~200 ms before refresh because replay was never expired.

questions.promptHtml: Why does every Android sample use WhileSubscribed(5_000)? Where does 5 seconds come from and is it a rule?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you treat it as cargo cult or a deliberate trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "During a configuration change the Activity is destroyed and recreated within a fraction of a second, so the collector disappears and reappears. With timeout 0 the upstream would be cancelled and restarted on every rotation. A 5-second grace period absorbs that. The 5 s matches the ANR threshold for input events, a conservative upper bound for recreation, and it is not a rule; I tune it per upstream cost."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rotation timeline: onStop -> collector cancelled by repeatOnLifecycle -> subscriptionCount 0 -> pending stop scheduled -> new Activity onStart (typically tens to a few hundred ms, slower on low-end devices) -> new collector -> count 1 -> pending stop cancelled. ViewModel survives, so the sharing coroutine is intact.

The same grace period also helps when the user briefly goes to the app switcher, a permission dialog, or the next screen and quickly returns (within 5 s no restart, no re-query).

The 5 seconds is the figure the Android architecture guidance uses; its rationale is that it's long enough for config changes and short enough that a truly backgrounded app stops doing work (Android's own input-dispatch ANR timeout is also 5 s, which is where people often say the number was borrowed from; I treat that as folklore, not spec).

Tuning:

  • Cheap in-memory/Room upstream: 5 s is fine.
  • Costly or battery-heavy upstream (GPS, BLE scanning, high-frequency socket): lower (0-1 s) or accept a restart cost, and make recreation cheap (cached value).
  • Very expensive to restart (heavy computation): larger timeout, but consider caching instead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Tunable constant, not a magic number scattered across the app
object Sharing {
    val UiDefault = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000)
}
val state = flow.stateIn(viewModelScope, Sharing.UiDefault, UiState.Loading)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using 5000 for a GPS flow and burning battery for 5 s on every leave.
  • Using 0 for a network-backed flow and refetching on every rotation.
  • Thinking the value ties to some Android guarantee for recreation time. It does not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the activity is recreated after 6 s (slow device)? → Upstream restarts; with replay not expired, the old value shows first, so UX is OK.
  2. Does the timeout apply when the ViewModel is cleared? → No, scope cancellation ends upstream immediately.
  3. Alternative to a timeout? → Cache in repository and make restarts cheap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "5 seconds for rotation." Senior: explains collector-gap mechanism, says it's tunable, and picks different values by upstream cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fleet app on cheap tablets recreated Activities in ~1.2 s; 5 s was fine, but a custom 500 ms value caused repeated BLE rescans on rotation.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between stateIn(scope, started, initialValue) and the suspending stateIn(scope)? When is each appropriate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The suspend overload is rarely used correctly; interviewers want to see you understand blocking semantics and failure modes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The three-arg version returns immediately with an initial value and follows a SharingStarted policy. The suspend version has no policy: it starts the upstream eagerly in my scope, suspends until the first value arrives, and returns a StateFlow that is already populated. It throws NoSuchElementException if the flow completes with no value. I use the first in ViewModels, and the suspend one where I need a non-null initial state, such as a DI initializer or a test."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Overload 1: non-suspending, no wait. You provide a placeholder (Loading, emptyList(), null).
  • Overload 2: suspend fun Flow<T>.stateIn(scope): StateFlow<T>; upstream runs eagerly in scope for its entire lifetime. The caller waits for the first emission; no placeholder values needed, state type can be non-null T.
  • Failure modes of overload 2: upstream completes empty -> NoSuchElementException; upstream throws before first value -> exception propagates to caller (and also to scope as in any sharing coroutine); slow first value -> caller is blocked (don't call from onCreate on main without launching).
  • You cannot use WhileSubscribed with overload 2. If the upstream must stop, use overload 1.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SessionRepo(private val store: DataStore<Prefs>, appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    // Suspend variant: caller gets a populated, non-null StateFlow
    suspend fun sessionState(scope: CoroutineScope): StateFlow<Session> =
        store.data.map { it.toSession() }.stateIn(scope)
}

// ViewModel: non-suspending overload with placeholder
val ui: StateFlow<UiState> = repo.observe().map(::toUi)
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling the suspend overload in a ViewModel init on main without launch, serializing startup on disk/network.
  • Expecting restart/stop behavior from it.
  • Using it on a flow that can legitimately be empty.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid a fake initial value then? → Model the loading state explicitly in the type (sealed UiState), not a fake data object.
  2. Overload 2 plus cancellation of the caller? → Waiting is cancellable; check your scope handling, since the upstream lives in the scope you pass, not the caller.
  3. Why not first() yourself? → first() cancels the upstream after one value; the suspend stateIn keeps it running.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "one has an initial value." Senior: knows the empty-flow exception, eager lifecycle, and that no sharing policy is possible.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup path used the suspend overload on a DataStore flow synchronously on main, adding ~80 ms cold-start jank until moved off-main.

questions.promptHtml: stateIn vs shareIn: how do they differ in behavior, and how do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates over-use shareIn(replay=1) when they want state, or use stateIn for events and lose emissions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "stateIn produces a StateFlow: always has a value, conflates, drops equal consecutive values, .value readable. shareIn produces a SharedFlow: no required initial value, replay and buffer configurable, every emission is delivered (equal values included) subject to buffering. I choose stateIn for state the UI renders, shareIn for streams or events where each item matters or where there's no meaningful initial value."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect stateIn shareIn
Result StateFlow<T> SharedFlow<T>
Initial value required (or suspend until first) none
Replay exactly 1 (latest) replay param (0 default)
Equal consecutive values dropped (==) delivered
Slow collector conflated (only latest) buffer with overflow policy of the upstream's buffer chain
.value yes no (replayCache only)
Late subscriber gets current value gets last replay items

Buffer sizing for shareIn: the shared flow's extra buffer is derived from buffer(...) operators you put before shareIn (the docs recommend using buffer upstream); default is suspending the upstream when subscribers are slow (default BufferOverflow.SUSPEND). With replay=0 and no subscribers, emissions are dropped, because nobody is there (not suspended).

Gotchas: shareIn(…, replay = 1) is close to but not the same as stateIn: no distinct filtering, no initial value, no .value, and an expired replay leaves it empty rather than resetting to a placeholder.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// state -> stateIn
val price: StateFlow<Price> = ticks.stateIn(vmScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), Price.Unknown)
// stream where every tick matters (e.g. chart points) -> shareIn
val ticksShared: SharedFlow<Tick> = ticks.shareIn(vmScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), replay = 0)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using stateIn for a stream where equal consecutive items are meaningful (two identical "Retry" clicks).
  • Using shareIn(replay=0) for state: a late subscriber sees nothing until the next emission.
  • Believing shareIn(replay=1) is "StateFlow without initial value": missing equality dedup and .value.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a stateIn collector miss values? → Yes, conflation: only the latest is guaranteed.
  2. Can I convert later? → sharedFlow.stateIn(scope, started, initial) works since SharedFlow is a Flow.
  3. When does shareIn suspend the upstream? → When there are subscribers with full buffers and BufferOverflow.SUSPEND.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists "replay and initial value". Senior includes conflation/equality, buffer semantics, drop-when-no-subscriber behavior, and picks per data semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Using stateIn for an analytics stream silently dropped identical consecutive events, under-reporting taps.

questions.promptHtml: With stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), initial), I read viewModel.state.value from a click handler with no collector active. What do I get, and what are the implications?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes a very common bug source: assuming a StateFlow is always up to date.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I get the last cached value, or the initial value if the upstream has never run or the cache was reset. Reading .value doesn't subscribe, so it doesn't start the upstream. If the flow is only active while the UI is collecting, then any logic that reads .value from outside collection (in tests, in a notification handler, in onCleared) can see stale or placeholder data."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
StateFlow.value just reads the atomic field. subscriptionCount counts collectors only. Therefore:

  • First access before any collection: initial value (Loading), so if (state.value is Loaded) is false.
  • After upstream stopped: the last value (until replay expiration).
  • With Eagerly, .value is always fresh because upstream runs.

Cases that bite:

  1. Unit tests that assert viewModel.state.value without a collector (the test sees Loading forever; fix with backgroundScope.launch { vm.state.collect {} }, Q614).
  2. Business logic using .value of a derived StateFlow to decide a save/submit.
  3. Code in SavedStateHandle/analytics reading .value after the screen is gone.

Rule of thumb: UI-derived WhileSubscribed StateFlows are for rendering. For decisions, get fresh data via a suspend call (first() on the source, or a repository method), or keep a separate MutableStateFlow that the ViewModel writes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fragile: depends on someone collecting
fun onSubmit() {
    val cart = cartState.value            // may be EMPTY/Loading if no collector
    ...
}
// Robust: ask the source of truth
fun onSubmit() = viewModelScope.launch {
    val cart = repo.observeCart().first()
    ...
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating .value as authoritative.
  • Fixing flaky tests by switching to Eagerly instead of collecting in the test.
  • Thinking .value read from main is the issue; the issue is the upstream is off.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you make .value always fresh? → Eagerly/Lazily, accept the cost; or maintain a MutableStateFlow.
  2. Does first() on a WhileSubscribed StateFlow start the upstream? → Yes, first() is a subscriber, so it starts it and returns the cached value immediately for StateFlow (stale!), another trap.
  3. Different between replayCache and .value? → Same data; replayCache is a list view of it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE reads .value freely. Senior distinguishes render-state from decision-state and knows when upstream is not running.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout button read a derived WhileSubscribed total after returning from background and charged based on a cached price.

questions.subtopic: Why plain lifecycleScope collect is wrong
questions.promptHtml: Why is lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { ... } } considered unsafe in an Activity? What are launchWhenStarted and repeatOnLifecycle and why was the former deprecated?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who collect flows "so it works" from those who understand that background collection means background upstream work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "lifecycleScope is cancelled only at DESTROYED. So a plain launch { collect } keeps collecting while the app is stopped, wasting CPU/battery and updating views no one sees. launchWhenStarted suspends the coroutine below STARTED but does not cancel it, so the upstream producer stays active and keeps buffering; that's why it was deprecated in lifecycle 2.6. repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels the block on STOP and relaunches it on START, which cancels the upstream too."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three behaviors for an Activity going to background (onStop):

API Collector below STARTED Upstream (e.g. callbackFlow, DB observer)
lifecycleScope.launch { collect } keeps running keeps running; UI updates happen invisibly
launchWhenStarted { collect } coroutine paused (dispatch suspended) keeps running; producer buffers or suspends depending on flow
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { collect } cancelled cancelled (cold flow) / unsubscribed (shared flow)

launchWhenX is implemented with a PausingDispatcher: it queues resumptions until the lifecycle reaches the state. The coroutine's upstream, e.g. a callbackFlow whose listener is registered, never learns it should stop. Google deprecated the launchWhenX family in Lifecycle 2.6.0 in favor of repeatOnLifecycle/flowWithLifecycle. (Check your lifecycle version's release notes; the deprecation is a warning-level @Deprecated.)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: collecting while in background
lifecycleScope.launch { vm.state.collect(::render) }

// Correct
lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect(::render)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "StateFlow doesn't do work while in background anyway". The upstream behind a Eagerly/Lazily-shared flow keeps working; and the collector does render work.
  • Using launchWhenStarted because "it stops collection": it only pauses.
  • Putting repeatOnLifecycle inside onStart (lint warns; it nests relaunch logic).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does repeatOnLifecycle block the caller? → It suspends until the lifecycle is DESTROYED; code after it in the same coroutine does not run before that.
  2. What does a new START give the collector for a StateFlow? → The current value immediately (re-render).
  3. What did the old launchWhenStarted do to a Channel producer? → The producer kept sending into the buffer; items queued or the producer suspended when full.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use repeatOnLifecycle." Senior: explains the pausing-vs-cancelling difference and its effect on upstream resources.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen using launchWhenStarted on a socket-backed callbackFlow kept the socket open and buffering for hours in background.

questions.promptHtml: Show the correct way to collect a StateFlow and a one-time event stream in an Activity. What happens step by step through start, stop, rotation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you can narrate the coroutine's actual lifecycle, not just paste the snippet.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I call lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { launch { collect state }; launch { collect events } } }. On every ON_START the block starts fresh; on ON_STOP it's cancelled, cancelling the collectors; the next ON_START runs it again. On rotation the old Activity's scope is cancelled at DESTROYED, and the new Activity registers new collectors. The ViewModel's flows persist, so the StateFlow replays its latest value."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline for one Activity instance:

CREATED -> STARTED : block launched (collect #1)     StateFlow emits current value
STARTED -> CREATED : (ON_STOP) block cancelled       subscriptionCount -> 0
CREATED -> STARTED : block launched AGAIN (collect #2) StateFlow replays latest
...
-> DESTROYED       : repeatOnLifecycle returns, lifecycleScope cancelled

Consequences:

  • The block executes N times, not once. Do setup (adapter init, listeners) outside the block; only collection inside.
  • Every restart re-renders from the current StateFlow value, so render must be idempotent.
  • For a cold flow (Room), each START re-subscribes (re-query).
  • A SharedFlow(replay=0) event emitted while stopped is lost to that collector (design-level topic: see one-off events chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: MainViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        // setup views once here
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                launch { vm.uiState.collect(::render) }
                launch { vm.events.collect(::handle) }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing vm.uiState.collect { } then vm.events.collect { } sequentially inside the block (second never runs, Q603).
  • Putting non-idempotent work (e.g. analytics.trackScreenView()) inside the block so it fires on every return from background.
  • Calling repeatOnLifecycle from onStart(): it creates a new coroutine on every start, each living until destroy (duplicate collectors).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. repeatOnLifecycle(RESUMED)? → Collects only while focused; see Q605.
  2. Why lifecycleScope.launch outside? → repeatOnLifecycle is a suspend function and needs a coroutine; also it returns only at DESTROYED.
  3. Can INITIALIZED be passed? → No, IllegalArgumentException.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE writes the snippet. Senior narrates restart behavior, idempotent rendering and what is lost while stopped.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "screen viewed" analytics call inside the block double-counted every return from the background, inflating metrics by ~30%.

questions.promptHtml: How is repeatOnLifecycle implemented? What guarantees does it give around cancellation, ordering and thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about the primitive instead of memorizing; it reveals knowledge of observers, mutexes and dispatchers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It switches to Dispatchers.Main.immediate, adds a LifecycleEventObserver, and suspends the caller on a cancellable continuation. On the upTo(state) event it launches the block in a child coroutine; on the downFrom(state) event it cancels that child; on ON_DESTROY it resumes the continuation so the function returns. A mutex ensures the previous block fully finishes cancelling before the next one starts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Simplified from the library (androidx.lifecycle, Lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle):

suspend fun Lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(
    state: Lifecycle.State,
    block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit
) {
    require(state !== Lifecycle.State.INITIALIZED)
    if (currentState === Lifecycle.State.DESTROYED) return
    coroutineScope {
        withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) {
            if (currentState === Lifecycle.State.DESTROYED) return@withContext
            var launchedJob: Job? = null
            var observer: LifecycleEventObserver? = null
            try {
                suspendCancellableCoroutine<Unit> { cont ->
                    val startWorkEvent = Lifecycle.Event.upTo(state)
                    val cancelWorkEvent = Lifecycle.Event.downFrom(state)
                    val mutex = Mutex()
                    observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
                        if (event == startWorkEvent) {
                            launchedJob = this@coroutineScope.launch {
                                mutex.withLock { coroutineScope { block() } }
                            }
                        } else if (event == cancelWorkEvent) {
                            launchedJob?.cancel(); launchedJob = null
                        }
                        if (event == Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY) cont.resume(Unit)
                    }
                    this@repeatOnLifecycle.addObserver(observer as LifecycleEventObserver)
                }
            } finally {
                launchedJob?.cancel()
                observer?.let { this@repeatOnLifecycle.removeObserver(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}

(Sketch; exact code may differ by version. Verify in source.)

Properties:

  • Main thread: observer callbacks must be on main; Main.immediate avoids an extra dispatch.
  • Cancellation: if the caller is cancelled (e.g. lifecycleScope / view scope), the continuation is cancelled, finally block removes observer and cancels the job.
  • coroutineScope { block() } means the block waits for all child launches (your collectors), and a child exception fails the block and propagates to the caller.
  • Mutex: if block cancellation is slow (cleanup in finally), the next block waits instead of overlapping.
  • State mapping: STARTED -> ON_START / ON_STOP; RESUMED -> ON_RESUME / ON_PAUSE; CREATED -> ON_CREATE / ON_DESTROY (so the last is effectively cancelled at destroy).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting it to behave like launch (non-suspending). It suspends until DESTROYED.
  • Assuming block cancellation is instant: cleanup in finally delays the next START start (mutex), including withContext(NonCancellable).
  • Throwing in a collector: kills the block and propagates up, which crashes via lifecycleScope's handler.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the lifecycle is already STARTED when called? → The observer replays current state: it receives ON_START synchronously upon addObserver and launches immediately.
  2. Why a mutex? → Prevents two concurrent block instances during cancel/restart races.
  3. What's different on viewLifecycleOwner in Fragments? → Its lifecycle is the view's; DESTROYED when view destroyed, so the call returns then.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "restarts on start." Senior: describes observer + job + mutex + immediate dispatcher, and consequences for exceptions and slow cleanup.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A collector with 3-second withContext(NonCancellable) cleanup delayed restart after backgrounding; mutex serialization looked like a frozen UI until cleanup was moved off the block.

questions.promptHtml:
I have three flows to collect in one screen. Why doesn't this work, and what are my options?

lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect { render(it) }
        vm.events.collect { handle(it) }
        vm.title.collect { setTitle(it) }
    }
}

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a top-three real bug; collect suspends forever on infinite flows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "collect on a StateFlow never completes, so the first collect suspends the block forever and the later lines never execute. I launch each collector in its own child coroutine inside the block, or use flowWithLifecycle/merge/combine when the flows belong together."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
StateFlow and SharedFlow collections never complete. Code is sequential inside a coroutine. So line 2 and 3 are dead code. No compiler warning.

Options:

  1. Child launches (most common, independent collectors, one block):
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) {
    launch { vm.state.collect(::render) }
    launch { vm.events.collect(::handle) }
    launch { vm.title.collect(::setTitle) }
}
  1. Separate repeatOnLifecycle calls, each in its own lifecycleScope.launch (works, more observers).
  2. combine flows into one UiState in the ViewModel and collect once (fewer collectors, better atomic rendering).
  3. Helper extension:
fun LifecycleOwner.launchWhenStartedCollecting(block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit) =
    lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED, block) }

Order of children: all start in the order launched; with Main.immediate each collector begins collecting before the next launch line, so a StateFlow's current value is rendered synchronously first.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using .launchIn(this) and forgetting it already launches (it's equivalent to launch { collect }; valid and concise: vm.state.onEach(::render).launchIn(this)).
  • Having an exception in one child cancel the siblings: they share the block's coroutineScope.
  • Using async for collectors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test that all three collectors are active? → Instrumented test with ActivityScenario, emit on each and assert UI changed; or a lint in review.
  2. Is one collector per flow costly? → No; coroutines are cheap; the cost is in upstream.
  3. How is flowWithLifecycle relevant? → Single-flow sugar; see Q604.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE spots the sequential bug. Senior also considers merging state in VM, exception coupling between siblings and render idempotency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A settings screen silently never handled navigation events for months; the events collect was the second line in the block.

questions.promptHtml: What is flowWithLifecycle, how does it differ from repeatOnLifecycle, and what does the position of operators relative to it mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many only know the sugar; the operator-position subtlety is the senior part.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flow.flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle, minActiveState) returns a flow that only collects the upstream while the lifecycle is at least that state, cancelling and restarting it as the state changes. It's built on callbackFlow + repeatOnLifecycle. Operators placed before it are cancelled/restarted with the lifecycle; operators after it keep running (downstream) and only get what passes through. It's best for a single flow; for several, repeatOnLifecycle is clearer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Implementation (from lifecycle-runtime-ktx):

public fun <T> Flow<T>.flowWithLifecycle(
    lifecycle: Lifecycle,
    minActiveState: Lifecycle.State = Lifecycle.State.STARTED
): Flow<T> = callbackFlow {
    lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(minActiveState) {
        this@flowWithLifecycle.collect { send(it) }
    }
    close()
}

Semantics:

  • The returned flow is cold: each collector of it sets up its own observer.
  • Upstream is collected only in the active window. Between windows, the callbackFlow's channel stays open (no completion) until DESTROYED, when the flow completes.
  • Position matters:
flow.map(::expensive)                       // cancelled with lifecycle (good)
    .flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle)
    .map(::cheapUiMap)                      // runs only as items arrive
    .onEach { render(it) }
    .launchIn(lifecycleScope)               // coroutine itself lives until DESTROYED
  • Using it with launchIn(lifecycleScope) is the conventional replacement for launchWhenStarted.
  • Buffer: callbackFlow default capacity is BUFFERED (64), so a fast upstream while the collector is slow can buffer; use .conflate() carefully.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
vm.uiState
    .flowWithLifecycle(viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle, Lifecycle.State.STARTED)
    .onEach(::render)
    .launchIn(viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting heavy mapping after flowWithLifecycle and expecting it to stop in background.
  • Using it for many flows then losing track of lifecycle scope choice.
  • Forgetting that completion happens only at DESTROYED.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which should I use? → repeatOnLifecycle for multiple flows / blocks of work; flowWithLifecycle for a single-flow pipeline reading nicely.
  2. Is there extra buffering? → Yes, the callbackFlow's channel.
  3. Equivalent in Compose? → collectAsStateWithLifecycle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "same thing as repeatOnLifecycle." Senior: knows the callbackFlow implementation, operator-position semantics and the buffer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An expensive map was placed after flowWithLifecycle, so it ran in background for items already queued; moving it upstream fixed 12% background CPU.

questions.contextHtml:
A Fragment-based "Orders" screen (1.2M DAU) has two reported bugs: (a) Snackbar messages from the ViewModel never appear; (b) after navigating Orders -> Details -> back, the list sometimes crashes with NullPointerException: _binding must not be null from adapter.submitList ... in a lambda; Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions affected. Code:

class OrdersFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_orders) {
    private var _binding: FragmentOrdersBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!
    private val vm: OrdersViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind(view)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                vm.orders.collect { binding.list.adapter.submitList(it) }
                vm.snackbar.collect { Snackbar.make(binding.root, it, 2000).show() }
            }
        }
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() { _binding = null; super.onDestroyView() }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find all bugs, explain each mechanically, and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks right; maybe launchWhenStarted." Or only spots the second collect. Doesn't know the difference between fragment lifecycle and view lifecycle on back stack.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is snackbar a SharedFlow with replay 0 or Channel-backed? (determines loss on rotation); is Orders added with replace + back stack (fragment survives, view destroyed)? Reproduction rate and API levels? Any other coroutines holding binding?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship the crash fix first (null-safe/viewLifecycleOwner change), since crashes dominate; the snackbar is a functional bug.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) wrong lifecycle owner: lifecycleScope is the Fragment lifecycle, not the view; (2) sequential collects; (3) leaked old collector from first view instance; (4) snackbar flow type.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add logging in the collectors and count active collectors after back navigation; Layout Inspector/LeakCanary shows old FragmentOrdersBinding retained; unit test with FragmentScenario and moveToState.
  5. Root cause: (a) vm.snackbar.collect is line two after an infinite collect; it is dead code. (b) On Orders -> Details, the Fragment is on the back stack: its view is destroyed (_binding = null) but the Fragment lifecycle goes to CREATED, not DESTROYED. The repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) block was cancelled at the Fragment's ON_STOP, then on return the Fragment reaches STARTED again: onViewCreated runs again (new binding, new collector) AND the old repeatOnLifecycle from the first view relaunches too, since the lifecycleScope coroutine from the first call is still alive. Result: two live collectors per visit (growing with each return), duplicate work, and any item delivered to a collector in a window where the Fragment lifecycle is still STARTED but the view is already gone (e.g. detach/ViewPager2 off-screen pages, exit animations, fast pop) hits _binding!! while _binding is null. The exact window varies by navigation setup, which is why it is only 0.4% of sessions; I would confirm with logs rather than assume.
  6. Fix:
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    _binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind(view)
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            launch { vm.orders.collect { adapter.submitList(it) } }
            launch { vm.snackbar.collect { Snackbar.make(binding.root, it, 2000).show() } }
        }
    }
}

viewLifecycleOwner is destroyed with the view, so the block and its coroutine die with the binding. 7. Prevention: Lint rule/code review: in Fragments only viewLifecycleOwner for UI collection; lifecycle lint RepeatOnLifecycleWrongUsage (for calling inside onStart/onResume); a LeakCanary instrumented test; a ViewBinding property delegate that clears automatically. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrap with binding?. null-checks as the fix (hides duplicate collectors). Not use launchWhenStarted. Snackbar delivery semantics (SharedFlow vs events-as-state) is a separate design decision.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if Orders uses ViewPager2 with FragmentStateAdapter? → Same: fragment lifecycle vs view lifecycle differ for off-screen pages; viewLifecycleOwner is even more important.
  • Would lifecycleScope be fine in a plain Activity? → Yes, Activity lifecycle == view lifecycle there.
  • Does DialogFragment change it? → Its view lifecycle is still viewLifecycleOwner; same rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout fragment ran two copies of an observer after each back navigation; the "duplicate order confirmation" toast appeared once per visit made, growing with each return, and nobody linked it to lifecycleScope for a sprint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Misses both bugs or recommends null-safe ?. patches.
  • Hire: Finds sequential collect and the view-lifecycle issue, writes the correct fix.
  • Strong hire: Also explains back-stack lifecycle states, duplicate collectors, event delivery semantics and proposes lint/tests.

questions.promptHtml: In Jetpack Compose, what is the difference between collectAsState and collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and which do you use on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Compose candidates often assume composition is lifecycle-aware. It isn't, and the result is background upstream work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "collectAsState collects for as long as the composable is in composition, with no knowledge of the Activity lifecycle, so the flow is still collected after onStop. collectAsStateWithLifecycle (lifecycle-runtime-compose, stable since 2.6.0) wraps repeatOnLifecycle, defaulting to STARTED, so collection stops in the background and WhileSubscribed upstreams can shut down. On Android I use it by default; collectAsState is right in multiplatform or non-Android-lifecycle code."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
collectAsState is produceState + collect in a LaunchedEffect-like coroutine tied to composition. A stopped Activity usually still has its composition alive, so:

  • the coroutine keeps collecting,
  • subscriptionCount stays 1, WhileSubscribed never stops,
  • state writes still happen (recomposition itself pauses without frames, but the upstream work does not).

collectAsStateWithLifecycle semantics:

@Composable
fun <T> StateFlow<T>.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(
    lifecycleOwner: LifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current,
    minActiveState: Lifecycle.State = Lifecycle.State.STARTED,
    context: CoroutineContext = EmptyCoroutineContext
): State<T>
// Flow<T> overload additionally requires initialValue
  • Implementation: produceState(initialValue, this, lifecycle, minActiveState, context) { lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(minActiveState) { if (context == EmptyCoroutineContext) collect { value = it } else withContext(context) { collect { value = it } } } }.
  • For StateFlow it uses .value as the initial value so the first frame is correct.
  • While below STARTED, the State holds the last value; on return it resumes.
  • LocalLifecycleOwner source: in the Activity's content it's the Activity; inside a Fragment-hosted ComposeView it is the Fragment's view lifecycle owner.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun OrdersScreen(vm: OrdersViewModel = viewModel()) {
    val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    OrdersContent(state)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using collectAsState with WhileSubscribed and expecting background shutdown.
  • Calling collectAsStateWithLifecycle on a plain Flow without understanding that the initial value is a placeholder.
  • Collecting events via collectAsState (events as state is a design question; use LaunchedEffect + repeatOnLifecycle/LifecycleEventEffect for effects).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.flow.collect {} }? → Same non-lifecycle-aware problem.
  2. How do you collect a flow for side effects in Compose lifecycle-safely? → LaunchedEffect(lifecycle) { lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { flow.collect {...} } }.
  3. Does it work with Lifecycle.State.RESUMED? → Yes via minActiveState.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "lifecycle aware version." Senior: knows why plain collectAsState keeps upstream alive, that it uses repeatOnLifecycle, and where LocalLifecycleOwner comes from.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An all-Compose app moved to collectAsStateWithLifecycle and background CPU wakeups dropped as WhileSubscribed upstreams finally stopped.

questions.promptHtml: STARTED, RESUMED or CREATED: which state should I use for repeatOnLifecycle, and what goes wrong with the others?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of visible vs focused vs alive, and multi-window, dialogs and PiP.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "STARTED is the default: the UI is visible, so I collect. RESUMED means focused and interactive; it pauses when a dialog-themed activity or a system overlay partially covers my screen, and in older multi-window modes the unfocused visible app is only STARTED. CREATED keeps collecting while invisible, effectively the same problem as plain lifecycleScope until destroy. I use STARTED for rendering, RESUMED only for things that require interactivity such as sensors tied to user focus."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State Reached on Left on Notes
CREATED onCreate (and after onStop) onDestroy active while stopped, so background upstream stays
STARTED onStart onStop visible; works in split-screen for both apps
RESUMED onResume onPause foreground focus
  • onPause triggers when another activity partially covers you (translucent permission dialog, a dialog-themed Activity, split-screen where the other window has focus). Collecting at RESUMED would stop updates for a screen the user still sees. In multi-window, both visible apps are STARTED; since Android 10 (API 29) multi-resume allows both to be RESUMED on supporting devices, but you can't rely on it.
  • Picture-in-picture and freeform windows: the activity is visible; STARTED keeps content updating (verify in your target devices).
  • For sensors/camera/location prompting, tie to RESUMED only if product wants "active focus only"; otherwise STARTED.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { vm.live.collect(::render) }   // typical
repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.RESUMED) { vm.cameraFrames.collect(::draw) } // needs focus, e.g. exclusive camera

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using RESUMED to "be extra safe": UI goes stale beneath dialogs and in split-screen.
  • Using CREATED for the sake of "no restart", causing background work.
  • Passing Lifecycle.State.INITIALIZED (throws) or DESTROYED.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What state does a stopped Activity have? → CREATED.
  2. Why does the permission dialog matter? → System permission dialog activity pauses yours; you remain visible, so STARTED continues.
  3. Would you ever collect at CREATED? → Rarely: truly needed background UI-state work belongs in the ViewModel/repository, not a View collector.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "STARTED." Senior maps each state to onX callbacks and discusses dialogs, multi-window, and why background work is not a UI collector's job.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A live-score screen froze under a transparent permission-rationale activity because collection was tied to RESUMED.

A ride-hailing app (3.5M DAU) ships a map screen. Play Console / support show "location icon stays on after leaving the app" and a battery-drain complaint cluster: users report 8-12% extra battery per hour when the app is backgrounded. Android vitals flags "excessive wakeups". Code:

class MapViewModel(locationRepo: LocationRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val location: StateFlow<LatLng?> = locationRepo.updates()    // callbackFlow { requestLocationUpdates(...); awaitClose { remove } }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null)
}
// Fragment

questions.promptHtml: Why is GPS still on, how would you confirm, and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The collector is already in repeatOnLifecycle, so it must be a different bug." Or "Cancel it in onStop manually." Misses that the sharing policy, not the collector, controls the upstream.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the process stay alive in background (cached app, foreground service?). Which screens share the ViewModel? Is a foreground service legitimately tracking a trip? What OS versions (background location limits from Android 8/10)? Any other stateIn/shareIn on the location?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: change Eagerly to WhileSubscribed(…); staged rollout 5% -> 50% -> 100%; remote-config kill switch for update interval.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Eagerly keeps callbackFlow registered for the ViewModel's life; (2) ViewModel lives while the Activity is in the back stack/cached; (3) another collector (service, trip tracker); (4) awaitClose missing (verify first in code, it exists here); (5) fused provider config.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys location to list active location requests and package; Battery Historian/dumpsys batterystats; Android Studio Energy profiler; log in callbackFlow register/unregister; unit test that counts subscriptionCount / registration.
  5. Root cause: Eagerly starts collecting at ViewModel creation and stops only when viewModelScope is cancelled in onCleared. The ViewModel is retained while its owner (Activity/back stack entry) exists, including when the app is backgrounded. The UI collector disappearing doesn't matter because the sharing policy ignores subscriber count. Fix target: the policy.
  6. Fix:
val location: StateFlow<LatLng?> = locationRepo.updates()
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 1_000), null)

Timeout shortened to 1 s (not 5 s) because upstream is battery-expensive; the fragment's STARTED window covers visible time. Long-term: expose a LocationRequest priority matching need (balanced power when not following the user), and for real trip tracking use a foreground service with its own scope rather than a ViewModel. 7. Prevention: Code review checklist: every callbackFlow registering a hardware/system listener must be consumed through WhileSubscribed; an instrumented test using FakeLocationClient asserting unregister after ON_STOP + timeout; Play vitals alerts for wakeups; Energy profiler in release checklist. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on onStop manual cancellation (races, easy to forget). Not set timeout 0: rotation would unregister/re-register, causing a gap of location fixes and cold-start fix latency. 1 s costs ~1 s of GPS after leaving, small against complexity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if product wants the blue dot to jump instantly on return? → replayExpirationMillis stays default so the last location shows immediately, then fresh fix arrives; combine with getLastLocation() seed.
  • What if two screens need location? → Same ViewModel/repository flow shared via WhileSubscribed; count covers both, or an app-scoped shareIn in the repository.
  • What if the user starts a trip and leaves the app? → That needs a foreground service (with notification); that scope is explicit, not UI-bound.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A delivery app's location Eagerly flow was copied from an auth-state flow that genuinely needed Eagerly; nobody revisited the policy and the GPS icon bug survived two releases.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the collector or suggests manual stop calls only.
  • Hire: Identifies Eagerly vs WhileSubscribed, fixes policy, verifies with dumpsys.
  • Strong hire: Chooses timeout by hardware cost, discusses foreground service for real tracking, staged rollout and test/lint prevention.

questions.promptHtml: How does SharingStarted work under the hood, and when would you write your own strategy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you understand the sharing machinery is a command stream driven by subscriber count, not special magic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SharingStarted is an interface with one method: command(subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>): Flow<SharingCommand>. The sharing coroutine collects those commands: START begins collecting upstream, STOP cancels it, STOP_AND_RESET_REPLAY_CACHE cancels and resets the cache. I'd write a custom one when the stop condition isn't just subscriber count, like keeping the upstream alive while a foreground service is running, or while the app has network."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
public fun interface SharingStarted {
    public fun command(subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>): Flow<SharingCommand>
}
enum class SharingCommand { START, STOP, STOP_AND_RESET_REPLAY_CACHE }

Built-ins in these terms:

  • Eagerly: flowOf(START).
  • Lazily: wait until count > 0, then START (never stops).
  • WhileSubscribed: subscriptionCount.transformLatest { n -> if (n > 0) emit(START) else { delay(stopTimeout); if (replayExpiration > 0) { emit(STOP); delay(replayExpiration) }; emit(STOP_AND_RESET_REPLAY_CACHE) } }.dropWhile { it != START }.distinctUntilChanged().

Custom example: keep sharing alive while there are subscribers OR a "keepAlive" flag is on.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun whileSubscribedOrPinned(pinned: Flow<Boolean>, stopTimeoutMs: Long = 5_000) =
    SharingStarted { subscriptionCount ->
        combine(subscriptionCount.map { it > 0 }, pinned) { subs, pin -> subs || pin }
            .distinctUntilChanged()
            .transformLatest { active ->
                if (active) emit(SharingCommand.START)
                else { delay(stopTimeoutMs); emit(SharingCommand.STOP) }
            }
    }

val trip = repo.tripUpdates().stateIn(vmScope, whileSubscribedOrPinned(tripActive), Trip.None)

Rules of thumb: commands should be idempotent; use transformLatest so a new signal cancels a pending stop; return Flow that doesn't complete unless you want sharing to end.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Emitting STOP and never START again on re-subscription.
  • Blocking inside command (it must return a Flow quickly).
  • Writing custom when WhileSubscribed plus a different upstream (e.g. flatMapLatest on an "active" flag) is simpler.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternative to a custom SharingStarted? → Gate the upstream: active.flatMapLatest { if (it) source else emptyFlow() }.stateIn(..., WhileSubscribed()).
  2. How is subscriptionCount for StateFlow computed? → Number of active collectors, exposed as StateFlow<Int>.
  3. Does STOP lose data? → Cache stays, only reset command clears.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: knows the built-ins. Senior knows the command protocol and designs conditional sharing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A telematics app used a custom starter tied to "trip active" so a sensor flow continued during screen-off.
