A list of 250 chats; each recomposition of ChatRow calls unreadCount again.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use remember." Without recognizing the leak is in the ViewModel scope (stateIn never stops), or suggests WhileSubscribed as the full fix.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often do rows recompose (scroll, state changes)? Is the unread count in the same table as the list? How big is the DB (writes per minute)? Is there a way to fetch counts in a single query?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch Eagerly to WhileSubscribed(5_000) and cache by id as a quick patch, ship behind rollout. Better: stop calling the function per row.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) stateIn inside a function: each call creates a new sharing coroutine and a new Room observer in viewModelScope; (2) Eagerly means none of them ever stop until onCleared; (3) recomposition frequency; (4) Room invalidation fan-out: each write invalidates all N observers and re-runs N queries.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android Studio memory profiler heap dump counting StateFlowImpl/StartedLazily/coroutine instances; Perfetto showing many Room query threads after each write; coroutine debug probes (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines); log in unreadCount.
  5. Root cause: stateIn has a side effect: it launches a coroutine in the given scope. Putting it in a function that is called from composition means each call launches another collector of an independent Room query, all in viewModelScope. Eagerly never stops them. With 250 rows and each recomposition, hundreds of coroutines and DB observers pile up; each write fans out to all and saturates the Room query executor, blocking main-waiters indirectly (ANRs).
  6. Fix:
class ChatViewModel(repo: ChatRepository) : ViewModel() {
    // One query, one upstream: map of chatId -> unread
    val unreadByChat: StateFlow<Map<String, Int>> = repo.observeAllUnread()   // SELECT chatId, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY chatId
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyMap())
}

@Composable
fun ChatList(vm: ChatViewModel, chats: List<Chat>) {
    val unread by vm.unreadByChat.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    LazyColumn { items(chats, key = { it.id }) { ChatRow(it, unread[it.id] ?: 0) } }
}

Move the row to take a plain Int: stateless, previewable, no per-row collection. 7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no stateIn/shareIn in functions or getters (get() = ...stateIn) of a ViewModel; those must be properties initialized once. Add a test asserting subscriptionCount/active observers after N calls; Room query counters in debug builds. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not cache a Map<id, StateFlow> as the main fix unless per-id upstreams are unavoidable (still leaks with Eagerly; needs eviction). Not use Eagerly for per-item state. Whole-table grouped query trades some extra rows scanned for O(1) observers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if per-chat flows are truly required? → flatMapLatest on a selected id with one stateIn, or a bounded cache with WhileSubscribed in an app-scoped holder.
  • Would getter property val x get() = flow.stateIn(...) be the same? → Yes, a new sharing coroutine on every access.
  • Does produceState help? → It's lifecycle-bound to composition, but still an observer per row; the batched query beats it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tiny" fun stateFor(id) = ... .stateIn(...) helper copied from a docs sample created ~1,800 live DB observers in a long-running session; the fix was a one-line SQL GROUP BY.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests only remember or increasing thread pools.
  • Hire: Identifies the side-effecting stateIn in a function, fixes with a single property/query.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies observer fan-out, adds lint/test prevention, and explains Eagerly's non-stop semantic.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if the upstream of a stateIn throws? Which scope and handler receive the exception, and what do collectors see?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The sharing coroutine's failure semantics are subtle: the collectors are not where the exception surfaces. (Operators like catch/retry are covered in the error-handling chunk; this question is about the sharing machinery.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The upstream is collected by a coroutine launched in my scope. If it throws without catch, that coroutine fails like any child: with viewModelScope (SupervisorJob + Main.immediate) the exception goes to the thread's uncaught handler and crashes the app, unless I installed a CoroutineExceptionHandler. Collectors don't get the exception; the StateFlow just stops updating, and it doesn't restart even when new subscribers come, because the sharing coroutine is dead. So I put catch/retry upstream of stateIn and model errors as state."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• stateIn internals: scope.launchSharing(...) launches a coroutine whose body is upstream.collect { shared.emit(it) } (conceptually), started per the SharingStarted command flow.
  • Exception in upstream -> that coroutine completes exceptionally -> it is a child of scope.coroutineContext[Job].
    • viewModelScope has a SupervisorJob, so siblings are not cancelled, but the exception still goes to the context's CoroutineExceptionHandler or, if absent, the uncaught exception handler -> app crash on Android.
    • A plain Job() scope: parent and siblings cancelled.
  • After failure: StateFlow retains its last value; subscriptionCount changes no longer revive the upstream because the single sharing coroutine (which also handles START/STOP) is the thing that failed. So, even if you added WhileSubscribed, a thrown upstream permanently kills sharing.
  • Cancellation (not failure) is different: STOP cancels only the inner upstream collection job, and START creates a new one.
sharing coroutine (child of viewModelScope)
  |- collects SharingStarted commands
  |- START -> inner job: upstream.collect{ emit }   <- exception here fails the sharing coroutine
  |- STOP  -> cancels inner job (normal)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fragile: crash + dead StateFlow
val a = repo.observe().stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), UiState.Loading)

// Robust: handle upstream failure into state
val b = repo.observe()
    .map<List<Item>, UiState> { UiState.Success(it) }
    .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it)) }                  // upstream of stateIn
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), UiState.Loading)

Note: after catch emits the error the flow completes (upstream is finished); to allow recovery you need retryWhen or a trigger (see error-handling chunk).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping the collector in try/catch (exception never reaches it).
  • Assuming WhileSubscribed re-subscribing revives a failed upstream.
  • Swallowing CancellationException with a broad catch (see cancellation chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where would catch after stateIn go? → Nowhere: StateFlow never throws to collectors; it must be upstream.
  2. Does one failing stateIn kill others in the same ViewModel? → With SupervisorJob no, but the uncaught exception crashes the process anyway.
  3. How to make failing sources recoverable? → Wrap source in retryWhen, or expose a refresh trigger: trigger.flatMapLatest { source.catch{...} }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use catch." Senior knows who receives the exception, the crash path via SupervisorJob, and that the sharing coroutine stays dead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Room SQLiteException in a mapped flow killed a screen's StateFlow silently (with a handler installed), leaving a spinner forever until process restart.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (2.5M DAU) migrated its article screen from LiveData to StateFlow. After release 7.4: backend team reports /article/{id} request volume up 38% (from ~1,900 to ~2,600 RPS at peak), and users on tablets complain the article "reloads and flashes a spinner" on rotation. Android vitals unchanged. Code:

val article: StateFlow<UiState> = flow {
        emit(UiState.Loading)
        emit(UiState.Success(repo.fetchArticle(id)))   // network call, ~600 ms p50
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), UiState.Loading)

The Activity collects with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED). Tablet users rotate frequently; 11% of sessions have at least one rotation.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the extra traffic and the spinner, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cache the response in a variable" or "ViewModel survives rotation so shouldn't refetch": without noticing the sharing policy tears down the upstream at zero collectors.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the old LiveData version refetching on rotation? (No: it ran in init.) Is there an HTTP cache/ETag? How long does recreation take on affected devices? Does the traffic delta correlate with rotation/tablet share?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix with timeout; roll out by percentage; confirm via backend RPS dashboard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) WhileSubscribed() default stopTimeoutMillis = 0: rotation cancels upstream and restarts; (2) cold-start double fetch from process death; (3) other screens; (4) retry logic. Math: 2.5M DAU x ~4 article opens/day = 10M opens; if 11% of sessions rotate once, +~1.1M refetches/day ~ +11% of the load on average, higher on tablets/peak; rotation clustering on tablets and multiple rotations per session plausibly gives +38% at peak. Evidence needed from logs rather than math alone.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a log counter in the flow {} body; Charles/OkHttp logging interceptor on a test device rotating the screen; compare per-device-class request/open ratio in backend logs.
  5. Root cause: On rotation, the Activity is destroyed, its collector cancelled, subscriptionCount -> 0; with timeout 0 the upstream is stopped immediately; the new Activity subscribes again, restarts the flow {} body (which re-emits Loading and refetches). The initial Loading replay briefly shows the spinner. StateFlow keeps the old Success value cached, but the restarted flow emits Loading first, overwriting it.
  6. Fix:
.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

and remove the redundant emit(Loading) inside the flow (initialValue already covers it; emitting it again on restart causes the flash). Longer-term: repository caches the article (Room or in-memory with TTL) so restarts after the grace period are cheap; use ETag. 7. Prevention: A ViewModel test that simulates a collector leaving and returning within the timeout and asserts one upstream execution (Turbine + backgroundScope + virtual time, see testing chunk); define the standard sharing policy in a shared constant; dashboards for per-screen request-per-open ratio. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Eagerly (fetches even if screen never visible; background work). Not a huge timeout (30 s) to dodge the issue: wastes work in background.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rotation takes 6 s on a very slow tablet? → Upstream restarts once; mitigated by repository cache so the restart is not a network call.
  • User leaves for 20 s and returns? → Upstream restarts; with default replay the old Success shows instantly while refetch runs (stale-while-revalidate), if you don't re-emit Loading.
  • Should refresh-on-return be intentional? → Yes, then expose that as explicit refresh()/onStart semantic, not an accident of sharing policy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" LiveData-to-Flow migration doubled image-API traffic in a week; the cause was a single default parameter, and the vitals dashboards never caught it because nothing crashed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot connect rotation to subscriber count.
  • Hire: Identifies WhileSubscribed timeout 0, fixes with 5_000 and removes redundant Loading emission.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies traffic impact, adds repository cache and a regression test for upstream execution count.

questions.contextHtml: A trading app's portfolio screen uses stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), PortfolioUi.Loading) over a websocket-backed flow. QA files a bug: "when I come back to the app after lunch, I briefly see my old portfolio value from before lunch, then it jumps." Product replies: "That's expected, it's like a cached screen" while the risk team insists: "showing stale balances as live is a compliance problem." Another team wants no flicker on quick return (< 1 minute). Activities get killed rarely (ViewModel retained, process alive, ~35% of returns).
questions.promptHtml: How do you resolve the ambiguity and what do you ship?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set replay to 0" or "just show Loading" without discussing product semantics, or "the data is correct once the socket reconnects."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the maximum acceptable age of displayed data (seconds)? Does the UI show a timestamp / "as of"? Is staleness a legal requirement or a UX preference? What's reconnect latency p95 (~800 ms)? Are there degraded-mode requirements (offline)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop showing unlabeled stale data: introduce an "as of hh:mm" label immediately (UI-only change) while the proper policy is decided.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Default replayExpirationMillis = Long.MAX_VALUE keeps the last value forever; (2) websocket restart latency; (3) Compose/Views rendering the cached value before collector gets fresh data; (4) another cache layer.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log timestamps of cached value vs now on re-subscribe; test with fake clock; check subscriptionCount transitions.
  5. Root cause: Not a bug: the default policy retains the last StateFlow value across STOP. The question is which behavior we want. Time line (stop=5 s): last value remains until the scope dies unless replayExpirationMillis is set.
  6. Fix: Make staleness a product parameter:
val portfolio = socketFlow
    .map<Portfolio, PortfolioUi> { PortfolioUi.Live(it, asOf = clock.now()) }
    .stateIn(
        viewModelScope,
        SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 60_000),
        PortfolioUi.Loading
    )

After 65 s (5 s stop + 60 s expiration) the state resets to Loading; under that, stale-but-labeled data shows instantly. The UI also dims the value if asOf is older than N seconds (derived in UI via a ticker, not in stateIn). For compliance, order placement reads the freshest value through a suspend call, not the displayed cache. 7. Prevention: Put max-age in the domain model (asOf), unit-test the expiry with virtual time (advanceTimeBy(65_001)), and document sharing policy per screen in the design doc. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not replayExpirationMillis = 0 globally: users get a spinner on every quick return, hurting perceived performance. Not rely on UI-side timers for compliance. Not trust that "socket reconnects fast" as a safeguard.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does expiration apply while the user is looking at the screen? → No; it only starts after subscriber count hits 0.
  • What if the app stays on screen overnight with a dropped socket? → Replay expiry doesn't help; the model must carry connection state / staleness and the UI must show it.
  • What about process death? → ViewModel state is gone; initial value + persisted snapshot via repository.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A balance screen displayed a 14-hour-old value as current after unlock; no crash, but customer support got dozens of "my money is missing" tickets in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as pure bug, proposes a flag without asking requirements.
  • Hire: Knows replayExpirationMillis, asks for max-age, ships labeled/expiring state.
  • Strong hire: Separates display cache from decision data, tests with virtual time, defines staleness in the domain model.

questions.contextHtml:
A new engineer's ViewModel test passes locally with Eagerly but after the team standardizes on WhileSubscribed(5_000) it fails in CI with expected: Success(...) but was: Loading. 140 tests in 22 ViewModels fail. Test:

@Test fun showsItems() = runTest {
    val vm = ItemsViewModel(FakeRepo(listOf(Item(1))))
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(UiState.Success(listOf(Item(1))), vm.uiState.value)
}

ViewModel: val uiState = repo.items().map { UiState.Success(it) }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading). A MainDispatcherRule sets Dispatchers.Main to UnconfinedTestDispatcher().
questions.promptHtml: Why does this fail, and how do you fix the tests (and what would you NOT do)?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more advanceUntilIdle," or revert to Eagerly to make tests pass.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Main dispatcher and scheduler does the rule use? Are tests using runTest with the same scheduler? Do other tests assert emissions with Turbine?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Unblock CI by fixing the shared test helper rather than editing 140 tests individually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) No collector -> WhileSubscribed never starts upstream; (2) scheduler mismatch; (3) timeout needs virtual time; (4) fake repo emits only on collect.
  4. How I'd verify each: Print subscriptionCount; run with a backgroundScope collector; check Dispatchers.Main scheduler is runTest's scheduler.
  5. Root cause: .value read with no collector: the sharing policy yields no START, so the state is Loading forever. Under Eagerly it ran from construction, hiding the dependence.
  6. Fix:
@Test fun showsItems() = runTest {
    val vm = ItemsViewModel(FakeRepo(listOf(Item(1))))
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect {} }
    assertEquals(UiState.Success(listOf(Item(1))), vm.uiState.value)
}

// or with Turbine
vm.uiState.test {
    assertEquals(UiState.Loading, awaitItem())
    assertEquals(UiState.Success(listOf(Item(1))), awaitItem())
}

backgroundScope is cancelled automatically at test end (so no hanging). Make the MainDispatcherRule share the test scheduler (UnconfinedTestDispatcher() created in rule must be the same scheduler as runTest's; with Dispatchers.setMain before runTest, runTest picks up the Main's scheduler). Provide a shared helper fun <T> TestScope.collectInBackground(flow: Flow<T>). 7. Prevention: Test helper convention; lint/review: any StateFlow assertion needs an active collector; tests for stop-timeout behavior using advanceTimeBy(5_001). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not switch production policy to Eagerly for tests. Not use Thread.sleep or real delays. Not call advanceUntilIdle as a cure-all; it can't start something nobody subscribed to.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The test then hangs at the end? → The collector was launched on this (TestScope) and never cancelled; use backgroundScope.
  • How to test the 5 s timeout? → Collect in a job, cancel it, advanceTimeBy(5_000) -> upstream still active; advanceTimeBy(1) -> stopped (assert via fake repo's active-collector flag).
  • Why does UnconfinedTestDispatcher matter for the collector? → Eager start so the first emissions are not missed before assertions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" 100+ failing tests by flipping the policy to Eagerly in release code, and shipped a battery regression two weeks later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds sleeps/idles, changes production code to suit tests.
  • Hire: Collects in backgroundScope or uses Turbine, explains why.
  • Strong hire: Shares scheduler between Main rule and runTest, tests the timeout with virtual time, centralizes helper.

questions.contextHtml: A stock-quote app has a websocket feed (one subscription per symbol, server limit 5 concurrent subscriptions/user, server cost ~$0.002 per 1,000 subscription-minutes). Five screens (watchlist, detail, chart, alerts, widget host) observe the same symbols. Today each ViewModel does quoteRepo.quotes(symbol).stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), null). At 600k DAU, backend sees ~4.1 subscriptions per active user and users with large watchlists get 429s. Product wants 10x symbols (watchlists up to 50 symbols) next quarter.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the sharing layer. Where do shareIn/stateIn live, with which policy and scope, and what are the risks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the repository a singleton and use Eagerly," or "add retries on 429." Ignores per-symbol multiplexing and lifecycle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the feed per-user authenticated? Which screens can be alive simultaneously? Can the server multiplex symbols on one socket? What freshness is needed when the app is backgrounded (none)? What's reconnect behavior?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap and dedupe client-side: single shared flow per symbol to cut subscriptions to ~1 per symbol, treat 429 with backoff, ship quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) duplicate per-ViewModel subscriptions (confirmed by 4.1x); (2) Eagerly/long timeouts elsewhere; (3) retry storms on reconnect; (4) widget host keeps a socket in background.
  4. How I'd verify each: Server logs of subscription counts per user per symbol; client counter on registers/unregisters; Perfetto/network profiler for socket frames.
  5. Root cause: Sharing is per ViewModel, so N screens = N upstreams per symbol. Multicast must live below the ViewModels.
  6. Fix: A repository-level multiplexer in an application-scoped (Hilt singleton) scope:
@Singleton
class QuoteRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val socket: QuoteSocket,
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope
) {
    private val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<String, SharedFlow<Quote>>()

    fun quotes(symbol: String): Flow<Quote> = cache.getOrPut(symbol) {
        socket.subscribe(symbol)   // callbackFlow, unsubscribes in awaitClose
            .shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 3_000), replay = 1)
    }
}

Per symbol one upstream, shared by every screen; WhileSubscribed means no screen = no socket. ViewModels use stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) on top, which is cheap (in-memory). Reconnect/backoff lives inside socket.subscribe or a retryWhen. For 50 symbols, a batch API (single socket frame subscribing many symbols) via one shared multiplexed flow + filter. 7. Prevention: Metrics: active subscriptions per user (client) and server; a synthetic test with 5 fake screens asserting one register; lint on stateIn(Eagerly) for system resources. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: cache grows with symbols (bounded by user watchlists; evict is implicit because flows hold no resources when unsubscribed, only objects). App-scoped scope lifetime = process; make sure it's a SupervisorJob with an exception handler or the shared upstream crash takes down the app. Not Eagerly at app scope: leaves sockets open in background.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why replay = 1 for shareIn and not stateIn? → No sensible initial value per symbol; a late subscriber gets the last quote, otherwise waits for the next.
  • Widget host updates in background? → Needs WorkManager/foreground policy; not this layer.
  • Memory for 5k cached symbol flows? → Each is a small object; unsubscribed ones hold only the replay value, bounded and cheap vs sockets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving sharing from ViewModel to repository level cut upstream connections by about 75% and removed a recurring 429 incident at the cost of one carefully-scoped singleton.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as retry/backoff problem.
  • Hire: Identifies per-VM duplication, proposes repository-level shareIn with WhileSubscribed.
  • Strong hire: Handles scope/exception policy, multiplexing at 10x, cache growth, tests and metrics.

questions.promptHtml: With shareIn, what happens when a subscriber is slow? How do replay, buffer operators and BufferOverflow interact, and what does it mean for a shared upstream like a sensor or a socket?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: One slow collector in a shared flow can stall every other collector, a classic hot-flow production problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A SharedFlow with BufferOverflow.SUSPEND suspends the emitter when any subscriber's buffer is full, so one slow subscriber slows everyone, and the upstream producer. With no buffer operator, shareIn has no extra buffer; emission waits for slow subscribers. I put .buffer(capacity, DROP_OLDEST) or .conflate() before shareIn when freshness matters, which becomes the SharedFlow's buffer policy. With zero subscribers and replay=0, values are dropped."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MutableSharedFlow(replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow): total buffer = replay + extra. SUSPEND (default): emit suspends when slowest subscriber is behind by the full buffer. DROP_OLDEST / DROP_LATEST: never suspends.
  • shareIn creates the underlying MutableSharedFlow and derives buffer parameters from the upstream's buffering operators (buffer, conflate) placed directly before it; plain shareIn uses replay only. (Documented in shareIn KDoc; check your kotlinx.coroutines version for exact fusion behavior.)
  • conflate() before shareIn = buffer(CONFLATED) -> DROP_OLDEST with capacity 1: fast producer never waits, slow subscribers see latest only.
  • stateIn is always conflated, never stalls.
  • Subscribers are independent only when the buffer is large; otherwise they're coupled through the slowest.
upstream -> [SharedFlow buffer: replay + extra]
                 |-> fast collector
                 |-> slow collector  (SUSPEND: upstream waits for it)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Sensor stream: freshness over completeness, never block the producer
val accel = sensorFlow
    .buffer(capacity = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
    .shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(2_000), replay = 1)

// Chat messages: must not drop; accept coupling, buffer generously
val msgs = socketFlow
    .buffer(256)   // SUSPEND on overflow
    .shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the default SUSPEND on a high-rate sensor feed shared with a slow UI collector, throttling sensors.
  • DROP_LATEST on events where the newest is the important one.
  • Believing each subscriber has its own buffer (the buffer is shared, with per-subscriber position).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about collectLatest on the slow collector? → Cancels its own handler for each new item; reduces its lag but doesn't change the buffer policy.
  2. Is a subscriber with a heavy onEach + flowOn safer? → flowOn adds its own channel buffer for that collector (see flowOn chunk).
  3. How to detect stalls? → Time emit; log subscriptionCount; Perfetto slices on producer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: knows replay. Senior explains shared buffer coupling, how buffer operators configure shareIn, and picks overflow policy by data semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A telemetry feed shared by a chart and a logger stalled the sensor callback thread whenever the logger hit disk I/O.

questions.contextHtml: A large app (6M DAU, 40 ViewModels) has stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ...) everywhere. The company wants to move to WhileSubscribed(5_000) to cut background battery and DB load (Android vitals: background CPU wakeups above peer median). Past incidents: unit tests relying on .value, a few ViewModels read .value in click handlers, one screen has an analytics side effect inside a map. Release train is weekly, rollback is hard once released.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan the migration safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Find and replace Eagerly with WhileSubscribed." Misses .value reads, hidden side effects, test breakage and the rollout plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which flows have side effects or non-idempotent upstream work (analytics, writes)? Which ViewModels are shared across destinations (nav graph scope)? Do any screens depend on pre-warmed data for first-frame UX? Is there a remote-config framework to gate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None is urgent; first, measure: baseline wakeups, background DB queries, startup/first-content time per screen.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (1) .value readers see initial data; (2) first-frame latency regression (lost pre-warm); (3) side effects in upstream now run per start/stop; (4) tests break; (5) shared ViewModels' count semantics.
  4. How I'd verify each: Static search for .value on migrated properties (Android Studio "Find usages" / custom lint); upstream execution-count tests; compare TTFC (time to first content) via macrobenchmarks/Perfetto; compare wakeups in vitals per cohort.
  5. Root cause: Not an incident: Eagerly was chosen for convenience; the migration changes liveness semantics, and anything implicitly relying on "always running" breaks quietly.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Add a shared factory/extension, e.g. stateInUi(initial) that wraps WhileSubscribed(5_000), driven by a remote flag for A/B (flag selects Eagerly or WhileSubscribed).
    • Migrate in batches by risk: pure read-only screens first; fix .value readers to use first()/repository calls; move side effects out of map into explicit onEach in a long-lived place or into repository.
    • Pre-warm where UX needs it: keep a repository cache so restart is cheap rather than keeping upstream on.
    • Tests: update helper to collect in backgroundScope; add tests for timeout behavior.
    • Rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over two or three trains, watch TTFC, crash-free rate, wakeups, support tickets; rollback via flag (no release needed).
  7. Prevention: Lint rule banning raw SharingStarted.Eagerly/Lazily in ViewModels without justification annotation; code review template; dashboards by screen.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not big-bang. Not disable pre-warm for every screen (some first-frame latencies will regress; repository caches pay for it). Not combine with unrelated refactors in the same release.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A screen's first paint regressed 120 ms? → Add a repository-level cache or a bounded Lazily for that single flow and document why.
  • Flag flipping at runtime? → Not mid-session; read at ViewModel creation.
  • Savings measurement? → Cohort comparison on wakeups per DAU-hour and battery stats; expect modest, so pre-agree thresholds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A policy migration surfaced an analytics event hidden inside a map that had fired once per Eagerly start; after migrating it fired per return, and a funnel metric doubled overnight.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Global search/replace.
  • Hire: Spots .value, tests, side effects; proposes staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: Flag-gated migration, repository caching to protect UX, lint for the future, measurable success criteria.
